content: 1. In 2014, Salanti et al. published a study in PLOS One that focused on assessing the quality of evidence derived from network meta-analyses. This work is critical for understanding the reliability of comparative effectiveness research in medical interventions. 2. Stahl and Berger, in a 1999 study published in Diabetes Medicine, reported a higher incidence of severe hypoglycemia requiring hospital admission in patients with Type 2 diabetes treated with long-acting sulfonylureas compared to those treated with short-acting sulfonylureas. 3. Van Staa et al., in a 1997 study in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, analyzed the rates of hypoglycemia among users of sulfonylureas, providing valuable insights into the safety profiles of these medications. 4. Zinman et al., in a landmark 2015 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, demonstrated that empagliflozin significantly improved cardiovascular outcomes and reduced mortality in patients with Type 2 diabetes, marking a major advancement in diabetes care. 5. Beale et al., in a 2006 study in Pharmacoeconomics, evaluated the cost-effectiveness of rosiglitazone combination therapy for managing Type 2 diabetes in the UK, highlighting the economic considerations of diabetes treatment strategies. 6. Erhardt et al., in a 2012 study in Clinical Drug Investigation, compared the cost-effectiveness of saxagliptin and metformin versus sulfonylurea and metformin in treating Type 2 diabetes in Germany, using the Cardiff diabetes model. 7. Gordon et al., in a 2016 study in Diabetes Therapy, assessed the cost-effectiveness of alogliptin as an add-on therapy to metformin compared to sulfonylurea in patients with uncontrolled Type 2 diabetes. 8. Granstrom et al., in a 2012 study in Primary Care Diabetes, analyzed the cost-effectiveness of saxagliptin (Onglyza®) in managing Type 2 diabetes in Sweden, providing insights into its economic viability. 9. Sabale et al., in a 2015 study in Primary Care Diabetes, evaluated the cost-effectiveness of dapagliflozin (Forxiga®) added to metformin compared to sulfonylurea added to metformin in Type 2 diabetes patients in Nordic countries. 10. Shearer et al., in a 2006 study in Pharmacoeconomics, explored the lifetime health consequences and cost-effectiveness of rosiglitazone combined with metformin for treating Type 2 diabetes in Spain. 11. Klarenbach et al., in a 2011 study in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, examined the cost-effectiveness of second-line antihyperglycemic therapies in patients with Type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on metformin. 12. The UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) Group, in a 1995 publication in Diabetes, provided a six-year overview of Type 2 diabetes therapy, emphasizing the progressive nature of the disease and the need for multiple therapeutic approaches. 13. Turner et al., in a 1999 study in JAMA, reported findings from the UKPDS (UKPDS 49), showing that glycemic control with diet, sulfonylurea, metformin, or insulin often requires progressive intensification of therapy in Type 2 diabetes. 14. Aljabri et al., in a 2004 study in The American Journal of Medicine, conducted a randomized trial comparing the addition of pioglitazone or bedtime insulin to maximal doses of sulfonylurea and metformin in poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes patients. 15. Gerstein et al., in a 2006 study in Diabetic Medicine, conducted a randomized trial comparing the addition of insulin glargine versus avoiding insulin in people with Type 2 diabetes on minimal or submaximal oral glucose-lowering agents. 16. Houlden et al., in a 2007 study in Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice, evaluated treatment satisfaction and quality of life in patients using an early insulinization strategy with insulin glargine compared to adjusted oral therapy in Type 2 diabetes. 17. Vinik and Zhang, in a 2007 study in Diabetes Care, compared the health-related quality-of-life impact of adding insulin glargine versus rosiglitazone in Type 2 diabetes management. 18. Morillas et al., in a 2015 study in Patient Preference and Adherence, investigated patient and physician preferences for Type 2 diabetes treatments in Spain and Portugal using a discrete choice experiment. 19. Bøgelund et al., in a 2011 study in Current Medical Research and Opinion, explored patient preferences for diabetes management among individuals with Type 2 diabetes in Denmark through a discrete choice experiment. 20. Casciano et al., in a 2011 study in the International Journal of Clinical Practice, quantitatively assessed patient barriers to insulin therapy, providing insights into factors influencing treatment adherence. 21. Horvath et al., in a 2007 Cochrane review, compared long-acting insulin analogues to NPH insulin (human isophane insulin) for managing Type 2 diabetes, offering evidence-based guidance on insulin selection. 22. The FDA, in its guidance document for the industry, outlined the development of drugs and therapeutic biologics for the treatment and prevention of diabetes mellitus, emphasizing regulatory considerations. 23. Ewen et al., in their insulin price profile report, highlighted global variations in insulin pricing, underscoring the challenges of affordability and access. 24. Permsuwan et al., in a 2016 study in Applied Health Economics and Health Policy, evaluated the long-term cost-effectiveness of insulin glargine versus NPH insulin for Type 2 diabetes in Thailand. 25. Beaglehole et al., in a 2004 article in The Lancet, discussed the role of collective action in improving public health in the modern era, emphasizing the importance of collaboration in addressing health challenges.
